summary: This Wikipedia-derived note covers several aspects of Dell Inc. in the late 2000s and beyond: its shift away from US manufacturing (plant closures in Austin, Lebanon, Winston-Salem and Limerick), its customer service troubles and recovery efforts, its growth and market position, its 2013 leveraged buyout, its retail distribution history, and its support brands. It also touches on Dell's board, its environmental pledges on PVC and flame retardants, and its earlier Austin headquarters.
one_line: Overview of Dell's manufacturing shifts, customer service efforts, market position, 2013 going-private deal, retail history and corporate governance.
key_facts: Dell closed its Mort Topfer Manufacturing Center in Austin, Texas (original location) and its Lebanon, Tennessee plant (opened in 1999) in 2008 and early 2009, respectively.
The Winston-Salem, North Carolina desktop plant received US$280 million in incentives from the state, opened in 2005, and ceased operations in November 2010.
On January 8, 2009, Dell announced the closure of its Limerick, Ireland manufacturing plant with the loss of 1,900 jobs, with production moving to its plant in Łodź, Poland.
Dell surpassed Compaq to become the largest PC manufacturer in 1999.
Operating costs made up only 10 percent of Dell's $35 billion in revenue in 2002, compared with 21 percent at Hewlett-Packard, 25 percent at Gateway, and 46 percent at Cisco.
In 2006, Dell spent more than $100 million on customer service improvements and later increased that spending to $150 million.
Dell's Direct2Dell blog started in July 2006, and Michael Dell launched IdeaStorm.com in February 2007.

Dell was the first company to publicly state a timeline for eliminating polyvinyl chloride (PVC) and brominated flame retardants (BFRs), and it launched PVC- and BFR-free G-Series monitors (G2210 and G2410) in 2009.
Greenpeace activists protested at Dell offices in Bangalore, Amsterdam and Copenhagen in March 2010, calling Dell's aspiration to be 'the greenest technology company on the planet' 'hypocritical'.
Dell opened plants in Penang, Malaysia in 1995 and in Xiamen, China in 1999, which assemble 95% of Dell notebooks.
In March 2013, the Blackstone Group and Carl Icahn expressed interest in buying Dell, and Blackstone withdrew in April 2013 citing deteriorating business.
Dell was taken private in a leveraged buyout that closed on October 30, 2013, ending its listing as NASDAQ: DELL.
In 2014 Dell was the third largest PC vendor in the world after Lenovo and HP, and it is the second largest non-oil company in Texas behind AT&T.
Dell stopped selling through Best Buy, Costco and Sam's Club in 1994 and resumed retail distribution in 2007, starting with Sam's Club and Wal-Mart.
Dell began manufacturing in Limerick in 1991 and at its peak employed about 4,500 people in Ireland.
